7DE5E38037BC4CD388771EE39ADB7A47.description: Understand the relationship between investment risk and return.

CD22F6C1DF1B4225AE358C43E0C24DEB.description: Explain the difference between a piggy bank and financial institutions.

0F41AB8B25584A29851DC7871ACDB487.description: Recognize various ways to save and the reasons individuals decide to save.

5F354114FBC54D63BA930FCAA1383495.description: Recognize the role of adults in providing safety.

AE74798D217E4ED98FA3836E29411820.description: Explain how written notes, emails, or phone calls between school and home can help prevent misinformation.

F3C5AC6E4D124A809EE3D40F88D2F9CB.description: Recognize different types of non-insurance protection.

10B7DCCCB010447681D6B9F15A6981AA.description: Recognize ways people can lose possessions.

164B3FE5F3EB435CB80076AF11093CA3.description: Recognize that everyone has an identity.

824A46C867934174A27FE3AC227CEF55.description: Establish strategies for protection of identity.

982FFE14C91446508983C3B2EDCB83EB.description: Develop awareness that each person has an identity.

901745D785C44B76813E5E194A31CF12.description: Demonstrate that if loaned, an item should be returned.

D44C9661B9334B1CBEB3982781DE95DE.description: Explain that a borrowed item needs to be returned.

A20D1005CD65456F8F65F7B175F84A7A.description: Understand rights and responsibilities as borrowers.

EC624C1446004B279F8585D0764E8025.description: Recognize the concept of the money behind the credit.

1BBA516B2DB140BDBC5613B81E9A8874.description: Demonstrate an understanding of the concept of credit.

568E21A5688344B8A9EB718EFB9780D8.description: Identify the values of each type of money.

E1233554DA21471FBE7096662A2CFAF9.description: Distinguish different types of money (bills, coins).

2A311095CDD944AC975FB1CECB3D6E3D.description: Recognize sources of income for children such as allowances and gifts.

55E5F08A0FE24B0A8B8078146E0AA670.description: Identify the outcome of spending money.

C0285CA8441544C191A9AC2D7564BF75.description: Describe the exchange of goods and services as part of the monetary system.

4437D7EB3AD34C958EB2463EF76ECD53.description: Develop a realistic spending plan for financial independence.

D3F747A8254645BCA2DA9EFB5554D0E2.description: Identify monetary resources and distribution options for those resources.

D924AC9A72ED4327A645BCD6A791AA75.description: Know the importance of needs and wants.

EED1B8DD963B4B788E36FFB4F4E46474.description: Develop short-term and long-term financial goals.

1B9C1C4B084A4602BA450F22ADED39A3.description: Demonstrate the ability to set goals based on wants and needs.

document.title: Iowa Core Mathematics

25A9907FEA0948E89F10B3476A98C3E7.description: Design and use a simulation to generate frequencies for compound events.
comments: For example, use random digits as a simulation tool to approximate the answer to the question: If 40% of donors have type A blood, what is the probability that it will take at least 4 donors to find one with type A blood?

01A8F7722420446E9B24655311915570.description: Represent sample spaces for compound events using methods such as organized lists, tables and tree diagrams. For an event described in everyday language (e.g., "rolling double sixes"), identify the outcomes in the sample space which compose the event.

CEE3294B3C6A4B0B817547B56AC9943A.description: Understand that, just as with simple events, the probability of a compound event is the fraction of outcomes in the sample space for which the compound event occurs.

10AEE434A7E1480D876293473F951F53.description: Find probabilities of compound events using organized lists, tables, tree diagrams, and simulation.

7128029C28184E81B53949AE52175416.description: Develop a probability model (which may not be uniform) by observing frequencies in data generated from a chance process.
comments: For example, find the approximate probability that a spinning penny will land heads up or that a tossed paper cup will land open-end down. Do the outcomes for the spinning penny appear to be equally likely based on the observed frequencies?

48AD53AF827243ECA9BF380C2036CE75.description: Develop a uniform probability model by assigning equal probability to all outcomes, and use the model to determine probabilities of events.
comments: For example, if a student is selected at random from a class, find the probability that Jane will be selected and the probability that a girl will be selected.

5A58B09B9EBA4ED396EC451DCFFE4845.description: Develop a probability model and use it to find probabilities of events. Compare probabilities from a model to observed frequencies; if the agreement is not good, explain possible sources of the discrepancy.

39E91BC9913E44768731E41C451C4DB2.description: Approximate the probability of a chance event by collecting data on the chance process that produces it and observing its long-run relative frequency, and predict the approximate relative frequency given the probability.
comments: For example, when rolling a number cube 600 times, predict that a 3 or 6 would be rolled roughly 200 times, but probably not exactly 200 times.

E8184A30D63D48388D5E4EDC67E6036A.description: Understand that the probability of a chance event is a number between 0 and 1 that expresses the likelihood of the event occurring. Larger numbers indicate greater likelihood. A probability near 0 indicates an unlikely event, a probability around 1/2 indicates an event that is neither unlikely nor likely, and a probability near 1 indicates a likely event.

75EF8B579A1D4D81A827E5BAF2EC948D.description: Investigate chance processes and develop, use, and evaluate probability models.

F1C71A01C51E4F8CA8E12A5DD0CC0587.description: Use measures of center and measures of variability for numerical data from random samples to draw informal comparative inferences about two populations.
comments: For example, decide whether the words in a chapter of a seventh-grade science book are generally longer than the words in a chapter of a fourth-grade science book.

1A7B4815E349412BABB0618DB90AF619.description: Informally assess the degree of visual overlap of two numerical data distributions with similar variabilities, measuring the difference between the centers by expressing it as a multiple of a measure of variability.
comments: For example, the mean height of players on the basketball team is 10 cm greater than the mean height of players on the soccer team, about twice the variability (mean absolute deviation) on either team; on a dot plot, the separation between the two distributions of heights is noticeable.

10FEAF448D4F4C8F86A6B5784A237851.description: Draw informal comparative inferences about two populations.

B29A05902C1649B387FF7E22E2A4437D.description: Use data from a random sample to draw inferences about a population with an unknown characteristic of interest. Generate multiple samples (or simulated samples) of the same size to gauge the variation in estimates or predictions.
comments: For example, estimate the mean word length in a book by randomly sampling words from the book; predict the winner of a school election based on randomly sampled survey data. Gauge how far off the estimate or prediction might be.

7C4FBB599CC3467784343B18B70585FB.description: Understand that statistics can be used to gain information about a population by examining a sample of the population; generalizations about a population from a sample are valid only if the sample is representative of that population. Understand that random sampling tends to produce representative samples and support valid inferences.

A78222D1A7AE48D3A94E491CC74A3967.description: Use random sampling to draw inferences about a population.

A5D5331613004F03971E5EA4E166504A.description: Solve word problems leading to inequalities of the form px + q > r or px + q < r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Graph the solution set of the inequality and interpret it in the context of the problem.
comments: For example: As a salesperson, you are paid $50 per week plus $3 per sale. This week you want your pay to be at least $100. Write an inequality for the number of sales you need to make, and describe the solutions.

ACFC08A83EEC44A8A35278BA2CEC811E.description: Solve word problems leading to equations of the form px + q = r and p(x + q) = r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers. Solve equations of these forms fluently. Compare an algebraic solution to an arithmetic solution, identifying the sequence of the operations used in each approach.
comments: For example, the perimeter of a rectangle is 54 cm. Its length is 6 cm. What is its width?

F146364A9D524723B927BB1E6C76202D.description: Use variables to represent quantities in a real-world or mathematical problem, and construct simple equations and inequalities to solve problems by reasoning about the quantities.

FAFC56AB94B6405394A704E1505D8E2F.description: Solve multi-step real-life and mathematical problems posed with positive and negative rational numbers in any form (whole numbers, fractions, and decimals), using tools strategically. Apply properties of operations to calculate with numbers in any form; convert between forms as appropriate; and assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies.
comments: For example: If a woman making $25 an hour gets a 10% raise, she will make an additional 1/10 of her salary an hour, or $2.50, for a new salary of $27.50. If you want to place a towel bar 9 3/4 inches long in the center of a door that is 27 1/2 inches wide, you will need to place the bar about 9 inches from each edge; this estimate can be used as a check on the exact computation.

EA0E35B6825C486A9B661737CA22282A.description: Solve real-life and mathematical problems using numerical and algebraic expressions and equations.

307A4B921F01432A833F1FC0A1DAE29E.description: Understand that rewriting an expression in different forms in a problem context can shed light on the problem and how the quantities in it are related.
comments: For example, a + 0.05a = 1.05a means that "increase by 5%" is the same as "multiply by 1.05."

73D11E6955C549B59B19AAEA3BC93850.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add, subtract, factor, and expand linear expressions with rational coefficients.

EB2BBF3C6AA54FE7A7AD064B7EF39E61.description: Use properties of operations to generate equivalent expressions.

11A11567973B4520BBBCBAD600EBA01D.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving the four operations with rational numbers.
comments: Computations with rational numbers extend the rules for manipulating fractions to complex fractions.

700F89402E1B47BF917A171AE8D98E97.description: Convert a rational number to a decimal using long division; know that the decimal form of a rational number terminates in 0s or eventually repeats.

B682F991FCFC4A9D9B439933B9495B82.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide rational numbers.

06EB7114225B47E0A3386F9AF401371E.description: Understand that integers can be divided, provided that the divisor is not zero, and every quotient of integers (with non-zero divisor) is a rational number. If p and q are integers, then -(p/q) = (-p)/q = p/(-q). Interpret quotients of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts.

69A43C73FCD240E68033D63BEBF224C0.description: Understand that multiplication is extended from fractions to rational numbers by requiring that operations continue to satisfy the properties of operations, particularly the distributive property, leading to products such as (-1)(-1) = 1 and the rules for multiplying signed numbers. Interpret products of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts.

EE886E43971445C99CB83BFE939F2CC6.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division and of fractions to multiply and divide rational numbers.

B238BD251DEC4FE1926AFEFB7C820609.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract rational numbers.

3B4A969F1DFF495DBDC0E7C5360E03E6.description: Understand subtraction of rational numbers as adding the additive inverse, p - q = p + (-q). Show that the distance between two rational numbers on the number line is the absolute value of their difference, and apply this principle in real-world contexts.

6723B78701CE48B0B50F557414997514.description: Understand p + q as the number located a distance |q| from p, in the positive or negative direction depending on whether q is positive or negative. Show that a number and its opposite have a sum of 0 (are additive inverses). Interpret sums of rational numbers by describing real-world contexts.

D350B69A6660478AAC4138AF659E9739.description: Describe situations in which opposite quantities combine to make 0.
comments: For example, a hydrogen atom has 0 charge because its two constituents are oppositely charged.

4145CD625F3944729F47D3F7971B268D.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of addition and subtraction to add and subtract rational numbers; represent addition and subtraction on a horizontal or vertical number line diagram.

CF2425FDD8E349EEB917F2BF2A0186CF.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of operations with fractions to add, subtract, multiply, and divide rational numbers.

894B7B03831D44CD943D71862004322C.description: Use proportional relationships to solve multistep ratio and percent problems.
comments: Examples: simple interest, tax, markups and markdowns, gratuities and commissions, fees, percent increase and decrease, percent error.

04166EBEF6634DAB9AB0699EECB3106F.description: Explain what a point (x, y) on the graph of a proportional relationship means in terms of the situation, with special attention to the points (0, 0) and (1, r) where r is the unit rate.

comments: For example, if total cost t is proportional to the number n of items purchased at a constant price p, the relationship between the total cost and the number of items can be expressed as t = pn.

356F50A0D36940918FEF3EB7572075F3.description: Identify the constant of proportionality (unit rate) in tables, graphs, equations, diagrams, and verbal descriptions of proportional relationships.

829F02145C354C22A95289E2E7501090.description: Decide whether two quantities are in a proportional relationship, e.g., by testing for equivalent ratios in a table or graphing on a coordinate plane and observing whether the graph is a straight line through the origin.

D042EBB30DD34BECB7A9FBA5ED800C16.description: Recognize and represent proportional relationships between quantities.

C8F8B68BC14949589B76DA64EC6691BE.description: Compute unit rates associated with ratios of fractions, including ratios of lengths, areas and other quantities measured in like or different units.
comments: For example, if a person walks 1/2 mile in each 1/4 hour, compute the unit rate as the complex fraction <sup>1/2</sup>/<sub>1/4</sub> miles per hour, equivalently 2 miles per hour.

C372B847F50643D19A6A5F1315A4B836.description: Analyze proportional relationships and use them to solve real-world and mathematical problems.

1FBB53138C024D4EB0BA6CAE45ECFCF5.description: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving area, volume and surface area of two- and three-dimensional objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons, cubes, and right prisms.

A5AA51D413974C2991C0D0213AD98337.description: Use facts about supplementary, complementary, vertical, and adjacent angles in a multi-step problem to write and solve simple equations for an unknown angle in a figure.

D16E85E0AE28485E9F52AF3C9AEA1384.description: Know the formulas for the area and circumference of a circle and use them to solve problems; give an informal derivation of the relationship between the circumference and area of a circle.

F89C642586A242BEAC27E18D44F1DD0C.description: Solve real-life and mathematical problems involving angle measure, area, surface area, and volume.

1455CAAEB84640ABBC27587801C1C975.description: Describe the two-dimensional figures that result from slicing three-dimensional figures, as in plane sections of right rectangular prisms and right rectangular pyramids.

F4EF9A8CA02E49C0A95FCA939EBEB83D.description: Draw (freehand, with ruler and protractor, and with technology) geometric shapes with given conditions. Focus on constructing triangles from three measures of angles or sides, noticing when the conditions determine a unique triangle, more than one triangle, or no triangle.

F203A07831CD4A89833A9198E1D44F4D.description: Solve problems involving scale drawings of geometric figures, including computing actual lengths and areas from a scale drawing and reproducing a scale drawing at a different scale.

51B004BD61B64DF3B105538D41133308.description: Draw, construct, and describe geometrical figures and describe the relationships between them.

733884195BED4D508CB8882AEFAD6A31.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

63C13ED0DDAA4C30901D4FBB1A246E52.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

E954246650E24FF8B3AD5B0C922DDBEB.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

E0EE061AA48142E39669692EE68E4D17.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Iowa Core Mathematics

5C091033092C4964A209FA1054A91645.description: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares, describe the shares using the words halves, fourths, and quarters, and use the phrases half of, fourth of, and quarter of. Describe the whole as two of, or four of the shares. Understand for these examples that decomposing into more equal shares creates smaller shares.

EA54D261E75F40BFBDDA888E4A825EF1.description: Compose two-dimensional shapes (rectangles, squares, trapezoids, triangles, half-circles, and quarter-circles) or three-dimensional shapes (cubes, right rectangular prisms, right circular cones, and right circular cylinders) to create a composite shape, and compose new shapes from the composite shape.
comments: Students do not need to learn formal names such as "right rectangular prism."

FA09BECF763542A7A3DD156E574074AF.description: Distinguish between defining attributes (e.g., triangles are closed and three-sided) versus non-defining attributes (e.g., color, orientation, overall size); build and draw shapes to possess defining attributes.

6A6FB13625D848B9ACE48E43BA4E2F44.description: Reason with shapes and their attributes.

B1329C9B0F6F4C0BA61AE184878F3B20.description: Organize, represent, and interpret data with up to three categories; ask and answer questions about the total number of data points, how many in each category, and how many more or less are in one category than in another.

C0F9DB0EA9D34CD9BF96496B21A4191A.description: Tell and write time in hours and half-hours using analog and digital clocks.

BC681389E11F45ADB4E939773F0B8FF4.description: Express the length of an object as a whole number of length units, by laying multiple copies of a shorter object (the length unit) end to end; understand that the length measurement of an object is the number of same-size length units that span it with no gaps or overlaps.
comments: Limit to contexts where the object being measured is spanned by a whole number of length units with no gaps or overlaps.

CE63F9E8B90D4705AF7452A92D15FCDC.description: Order three objects by length; compare the lengths of two objects indirectly by using a third object.

78552A09FFAF4F7E87C3D3E1DE46FA71.description: Measure lengths indirectly and by iterating length units.

CF20EFB6C6FB4F4983FD40E8BE4C8640.description: Subtract multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 from multiples of 10 in the range 10-90 (positive or zero differences), using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used.

AB9B0932B1304AA688F2B1BFC647C1F8.description: Given a two-digit number, mentally find 10 more or 10 less than the number, without having to count; explain the reasoning used.

6762629DE7604179B3CD5C9558E655B6.description: Add within 100, including adding a two-digit number and a one-digit number, and adding a two-digit number and a multiple of 10, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used. Understand that in adding two-digit numbers, one adds tens and tens, ones and ones; and sometimes it is necessary to compose a ten.

12907CAA1F3A4DE7A649AE8F79C9DB5B.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to add and subtract.

E779C84853024B3784B97AE971CCBBCF.description: Compare two two-digit numbers based on meanings of the tens and ones digits, recording the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, and <.

3E19F77631394F3FB3685BDA6A218B2E.description: The numbers 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 refer to one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine tens (and 0 ones).

0342B4666EBE4F539D6297C93867C122.description: The numbers from 11 to 19 are composed of a ten and one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine ones.

600ACBF2534E46FF95A1F0DE70F06614.description: 10 can be thought of as a bundle of ten ones — called a "ten."

117A450AE0DB4648951C4BDBD096A54F.description: Understand that the two digits of a two-digit number represent amounts of tens and ones. Understand the following as special cases:

2E13557EC44D4A56BB6402D1DE0B53C3.description: Count to 120, starting at any number less than 120. In this range, read and write numerals and represent a number of objects with a written numeral.

9FD477394ED046FE9FF0A0711BF66883.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

15DF79789EEA415DBDAC1E6BAA712E82.description: Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers.
comments: For example, determine the unknown number that makes the equation true in each of the equations 8 + ? = 11, 5 = - 3, 6 + 6 = .

21B384A2475B4364B2ABAA912B52ACCE.description: Understand the meaning of the equal sign, and determine if equations involving addition and subtraction are true or false.
comments: For example, which of the following equations are true and which are false? 6 = 6, 7 = 8 - 1, 5 + 2 = 2 + 5, 4 + 1 = 5 + 2.

25DBFDD5AAC940968EF281E2B5163387.description: Work with addition and subtraction equations.

F82DC04B9E3645969EBFCB3AA715153A.description: Add and subtract within 20, demonstrating fluency for addition and subtraction within 10. Use strategies such as counting on; making ten (e.g., 8 + 6 = 8 + 2 + 4 = 10 + 4 = 14); decomposing a number leading to a ten (e.g., 13 - 4 = 13 - 3 - 1 = 10 - 1 = 9); using the relationship between addition and subtraction (e.g., knowing that 8 + 4 = 12, one knows 12 - 8 = 4); and creating equivalent but easier or known sums (e.g., adding 6 + 7 by creating the known equivalent 6 + 6 + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13).

EF9D860EBA564376937947A50EDEC494.description: Relate counting to addition and subtraction (e.g., by counting on 2 to add 2).

5B53D4CDDDA846A7B98A3F665C945D8C.description: Understand subtraction as an unknown-addend problem.
comments: For example, subtract 10 - 8 by finding the number that makes 10 when added to 8.

51AA43E9C39345519AAE98416B1804DC.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract.
comments: Students need not use formal terms for these properties.
To add 2 + 6 + 4, the second two numbers can be added to make a ten, so 2 + 6 + 4 = 2 + 10 = 12. (Associative property of addition.)
If 8 + 3 = 11 is known, then 3 + 8 = 11 is also known. (Commutative property of addition.)

AE6BC40B44C84B9E85E8B776AC52753C.description: Understand and apply properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction.

5BE3E2D3E1FA410E9AA3346423247137.description: Solve word problems that call for addition of three whole numbers whose sum is less than or equal to 20, e.g., by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

6023F4B8FCD94A24865B2E178189C576.description: Use addition and subtraction within 20 to solve word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions, e.g., by using objects, drawings, and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

411FE3453F0A458392A703D5527FD5E1.description: Represent and solve problems involving addition and subtraction.

E9101AE8D2154EF68FB06993D2B8D39C.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

24826487A7424825B9670275AFDD0F2A.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

E9F5A94069974BDDADA19BBAF30457D5.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

58BE9ACD34934AD79A14777939F7E48A.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Iowa Core Science

BB991F30DFE50131AEB568A86D17958E.description: Make appropriate personal/lifestyle/technology choices, evaluate, observe, discuss/debate, recognize interactions and interdependencies at all levels, explain, describe environmental effects of public policy, choose appropriate course(s) of action.

BB98D870DFE50131AEB468A86D17958E.description: Integrated Standard: Science in Personal and Social Perspectives

BB989700DFE50131AEB368A86D17958E.description: Identify problem or design an opportunity; propose a design and choose between alternative solutions; implement proposed solution; evaluate solution and its consequences; communicate a problem, process, and solution; use computer software, device interfaces, lab equipment, calculators, and GPS; use presentation software and hardware, communications equipment, and remote sensing equipment; generate and manipulate data; describe the connection between technology and the state of current knowledge.

BB981340DFE50131AEB168A86D17958E.description: Identify questions and related concepts; design and conduct scientific investigations; use technology and mathematics; formulate and revise scientific explanations and models; recognize and analyze alternative explanations and models, communicate and defend a scientific argument, observe; experiment, measure, graph, evaluate, discuss/debate, research, collect/analyze data, imagine, diagram, concept map, engage in peer review, recognize experimental error, reflect, and predict.

BB978150DFE50131AEAF68A86D17958E.description: Understand significance of historical scientific events and technological advances; recognize/relate contributions of other cultures, groups and individuals; work as part of a team; build on work of others; engage in peer review; use logical arguments; rely on evidence; recognize/use new information; change hypotheses; identify/evaluate "great leaps"; recognize/evaluate what is and is not science.

BB973E40DFE50131AEAE68A86D17958E.description: Integrated Standard: History and Nature of Science

BB96FD20DFE50131AEAD68A86D17958E.description: Follow appropriate safety procedures when conducting investigations.

BB96ADB0DFE50131AEAC68A86D17958E.description: Students should communicate orally, through writing or through drawings.

BB9649B0DFE50131AEAB68A86D17958E.description: Students should begin to develop the abilities to communicate, critique, and analyze their work and the work of other students.

BB95ADB0DFE50131AEA968A86D17958E.description: Students' explanations should reflect the evidence they have obtained.

BB956F30DFE50131AEA868A86D17958E.description: Students should learn what constitutes evidence.

BB953150DFE50131AEA768A86D17958E.description: Use data to construct reasonable explanations.

BB94F2A0DFE50131AEA668A86D17958E.description: Students use tools such as rulers, thermometers, watches, balances, spring scales, magnifiers and microscopes to extend their senses and their abilities to gather data.

BB9471E0DFE50131AEA468A86D17958E.description: Students use tools such as rulers, thermometers, watches, balances, spring scales, magnifiers and microscopes to extend their senses and their abilities to gather data.

BB942A60DFE50131AEA368A86D17958E.description: Use tools to gather data and extend the senses.

BB93DFF0DFE50131AEA268A86D17958E.description: It is important to follow appropriate safety procedures when conducting investigations.

BB939CE0DFE50131AEA168A86D17958E.description: In earliest years, investigations are largely based on direct observations. As students develop, they design and conduct simple investigations to answer questions.

BB931780DFE50131AE9F68A86D17958E.description: Students should answer their questions by seeking information from their own observations, investigations and from reliable sources of scientific information.

BB92D640DFE50131AE9E68A86D17958E.description: Ask questions about objects, organisms, and events in the environment.

BB923DD0DFE50131AE9C68A86D17958E.description: An object's position or movement can be changed by pushing or pulling.

BB91ED60DFE50131AE9B68A86D17958E.description: An object's motion can be described by observing and measuring its position over time.

BB915090DFE50131AE9968A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply knowledge of the positions and motions of objects.

BB910880DFE50131AE9868A86D17958E.description: Some common materials, such as water, can be changed from one state to another by heating or cooling.

BB90AC70DFE50131AE9768A86D17958E.description: Materials can exist in different states – solid, liquid, and gas.

BB905580DFE50131AE9668A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply knowledge of characteristics of liquids and solids.

BB901460DFE50131AE9568A86D17958E.description: Objects can be described by the properties of the materials from which they are made. Properties can be used to separate or sort a group of objects or materials.

BB8FCF70DFE50131AE9468A86D17958E.description: Objects are made of one or more materials.

BB8F8520DFE50131AE9368A86D17958E.description: Objects have many observable properties including size, weight, shape, color, temperature and the ability to react with other substances. Those properties can be measured using tools such as rulers, balances and thermometers.

BB8F2E20DFE50131AE9268A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply knowledge of observable and measurable properties of objects.

BB8E92C0DFE50131AE9068A86D17958E.description: See 21st Century Skills of the Iowa Core Curriculum.

comments: Modeling is best interpreted not as a collection of isolated topics but in relation to other standards. Making mathematical models is a Standard for Mathematical Practice, and specific modeling standards appear throughout the high school standards indicated by a star symbol (★). The star symbol sometimes appears on the heading for a group of standards; in that case, it should be understood to apply to all standards in that group.

29D6CC30817A42F7BD44DCD3C6AEC98B.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

1289E11DFA2141E5BE0C61BE71BC83DF.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

FD720816FF7B42D8BE8425B82D374207.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

ADDF675E091044189719C0F7743B7F5C.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: Iowa Core Science

BBED9880DFE50131AF6E68A86D17958E.description: Make appropriate personal/lifestyle/technology choices, evaluate, observe, discuss/debate, recognize interactions and interdependencies at all levels, explain, describe environmental effects of public policy, choose appropriate course(s) of action.

BBED4900DFE50131AF6D68A86D17958E.description: Integrated Standard: Science in Personal and Social Perspectives

BBECF8E0DFE50131AF6C68A86D17958E.description: Identify problem or design an opportunity; propose a design and choose between alternative solutions; implement proposed solution; evaluate solution and its consequences; communicate a problem, process, and solution; use computer software, device interfaces, lab equipment, calculators, and GPS; use presentation software and hardware, communications equipment, and remote sensing equipment; generate and manipulate data; describe the connection between technology and the state of current knowledge.

BBEC5B80DFE50131AF6A68A86D17958E.description: Identify questions and related concepts; design and conduct scientific investigations; use technology and mathematics; formulate and revise scientific explanations and models; recognize and analyze alternative explanations and models, communicate and defend a scientific argument, observe; experiment, measure, graph, evaluate, discuss/debate, research, collect/analyze data, imagine, diagram, concept map, engage in peer review, recognize experimental error, reflect, and predict.

BBEBD430DFE50131AF6868A86D17958E.description: Understand significance of historical scientific events and technological advances; recognize/relate contributions of other cultures, groups and individuals; work as part of a team; build on work of others; engage in peer review; use logical arguments; rely on evidence; recognize/use new information; change hypotheses; identify/evaluate "great leaps"; recognize/evaluate what is and is not science.

BBEB8EA0DFE50131AF6768A86D17958E.description: Integrated Standard: History and Nature of Science

BBEB41C0DFE50131AF6668A86D17958E.description: Use appropriate safety procedures when conducting investigations.

BBEAD920DFE50131AF6568A86D17958E.description: Students should become competent in communicating experimental methods, describing observations and summarizing the results of investigations. Explanations can be communicated through various methods.

BBEA8190DFE50131AF6468A86D17958E.description: Communicate and defend procedures and explanations.

BBEA3F80DFE50131AF6368A86D17958E.description: Students should develop the ability to listen to and respect the explanations proposed by other students. They should remain open to and acknowledge different ideas and explanations, be able to accept the skepticism of others, and consider alternative explanations.

BBE9FDD0DFE50131AF6268A86D17958E.description: Recognize and analyze alternative explanations and predictions.

BBE9BA70DFE50131AF6168A86D17958E.description: Students should begin to state some explanations in terms of relationships between two or more variables.

BBE97500DFE50131AF6068A86D17958E.description: Students should be able to review data from an experiment, summarize the data, and form a logical argument between cause and effect relationships.

BBE92640DFE50131AF5F68A86D17958E.description: Students decide what evidence should be used and develop the ability to account for anomalous data.

BBE8D630DFE50131AF5E68A86D17958E.description: Think critically and logically to make the relationships between evidence and explanations.

BBE887F0DFE50131AF5D68A86D17958E.description: Different models can be used to represent the same thing.

BBE83AE0DFE50131AF5C68A86D17958E.description: Models are often used to think about processes that happen too slowly, too quickly, or on too small a scale to observe directly, or are too vast to be changed deliberately, or are potentially dangerous.

BBE7E840DFE50131AF5B68A86D17958E.description: Developing explanations establishes connections between the content of science and the contexts in which students develop new knowledge.

BBE7A0C0DFE50131AF5A68A86D17958E.description: Students should base their explanations on observations and they should be able to differentiate between description and explanation.

BBE755D0DFE50131AF5968A86D17958E.description: Use evidence to develop descriptions, explanations, predictions, and models.

BBE70900DFE50131AF5868A86D17958E.description: Mathematics is used to gather, organize and present data and to construct convincing explanations.

BBE68090DFE50131AF5668A86D17958E.description: The use of tools and techniques, including computers, will be guided by the questions asked and the investigations students design. Students should be able to access, gather, store, retrieve, and organize data, using computer hardware and software designed for these purposes.

BBE63BC0DFE50131AF5568A86D17958E.description: Select and use appropriate tools and techniques to gather, analyze and interpret data.

BBE5F4F0DFE50131AF5468A86D17958E.description: Some investigations involve observing and describing objects, organisms and events; some involve collecting specimens; some involve experiments; some involve seeking more information; some involve discovery of new objects and phenomena; and some involve making models.

BBE5A970DFE50131AF5368A86D17958E.description: Understand that different kinds of questions suggest different kinds of scientific investigations.

BBE55130DFE50131AF5268A86D17958E.description: Students use appropriate safety procedures when conducting investigations.

BBE4E500DFE50131AF5168A86D17958E.description: Students formulate questions, design investigations, execute investigations, interpret data, use evidence to generate explanations, propose alternative explanations, and critique explanations and procedures.

BBE49150DFE50131AF5068A86D17958E.description: Students should develop the ability to clarify ideas that are influencing and guiding their inquiry, and to understand how those ideas compare with current scientific knowledge.

BBE44820DFE50131AF4F68A86D17958E.description: Students should develop general abilities such as making systematic observations, taking accurate measurements, and identifying and controlling variables.

BBE3DF00DFE50131AF4E68A86D17958E.description: Students understand that different kinds of questions suggest different kinds of scientific investigations.

BBE38E80DFE50131AF4D68A86D17958E.description: Design and conduct different kinds of scientific investigations.

BBE34880DFE50131AF4C68A86D17958E.description: Students should develop the ability to connect their questions with scientific ideas, concepts, and quantitative relationships that guide investigations.

BBE300D0DFE50131AF4B68A86D17958E.description: Students should develop the ability to refine and refocus broad and ill-defined questions. An important aspect of this ability consists of clarifying questions and inquiries and directing them toward objects and phenomena that can be described, explained, or predicted by scientific investigations.

BBE2BC90DFE50131AF4A68A86D17958E.description: Identify and generate questions that can be answered through scientific investigations.

BBE22D50DFE50131AF4868A86D17958E.description: If more than one force acts on an object along a straight line, then the forces will reinforce or cancel one another, depending on their direction and magnitude. Unbalanced forces will cause changes in speed or direction of an object's motion.

BBE1DC50DFE50131AF4768A86D17958E.description: An object that is not being subjected to a force will continue to move at a constant speed and in a straight line.

BBE19760DFE50131AF4668A86D17958E.description: The motion of an object can be described by its position, direction of motion, and speed. That motion can be measured and represented on a graph.

BBE15070DFE50131AF4568A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply knowledge of motions and forces.

BBE0F9A0DFE50131AF4468A86D17958E.description: The sun is a major source of energy for changes on the earth's surface. The sun loses energy by emitting light. A tiny fraction of that light reaches the earth, transferring energy form the sun to the earth. The sun's energy arrives as light with a range of wavelengths, consisting of visible light, infrared, and ultraviolet radiation.

BBE0AA70DFE50131AF4368A86D17958E.description: In most chemical and nuclear reactions, energy is transferred into or out of a system. Heat, light, mechanical motion, or electricity might all be involved in such transfers.

BBE04710DFE50131AF4268A86D17958E.description: Electrical circuits provide a means of transferring electrical energy when heat, light, sound, and chemical changes are produced.

BBDFF390DFE50131AF4168A86D17958E.description: Light interacts with matter by transmission (including refraction), absorption, or scattering (including reflection). To see an object, light from that object- emitted by or scattered from it- must enter the eye.

BBDFA870DFE50131AF4068A86D17958E.description: Heat moves in predictable ways, flowing from warmer objects to cooler ones, until both reach the same temperature.

BBDF5690DFE50131AF3F68A86D17958E.description: Energy is a property of many substances and is associated with heat, light, electricity, mechanical motion, sound, nuclei, and the nature of a chemical. Energy is transferred in many ways.

BBDF00F0DFE50131AF3E68A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply knowledge of forms of energy and energy transfer.

BBDEB8F0DFE50131AF3D68A86D17958E.description: Chemical elements do not break down during normal laboratory reactions involving such treatments as heating, exposure to electric current, or reaction with acids. There are more than 100 known elements that combine in a multitude of ways to produce compounds, which account for the living and nonliving substances that we encounter.

BBDE6B20DFE50131AF3C68A86D17958E.description: Substances react chemically in characteristic ways with other substances to form new substances (compounds) with different characteristic properties. In chemical reactions, the total mass is conserved. Substances often are placed in categories or groups if they react in similar ways; metals is an example of such a group.

BBDE1560DFE50131AF3B68A86D17958E.description: A substance has characteristic properties, such as density, a boiling point, and solubility, all of which are independent of the amount of the sample. A mixture of substances often can be separated into the original substances using one or more of the characteristic properties.

BBDDCDE0DFE50131AF3A68A86D17958E.description:
Understand and apply knowledge of:
  • elements, compounds, mixtures, and solutions based on the nature of their physical and chemical properties.
  • physical and chemical changes and their relationship to the conservation of matter and energy.

BBDD41E0DFE50131AF3868A86D17958E.description: Disease is a breakdown in structures or functions of an organism. Some diseases are the result of intrinsic failures of the system. Others are the result of damage by infection by other organisms.

BBDCF9E0DFE50131AF3768A86D17958E.description: The human organism has systems for digestion, respiration, reproduction, circulation, excretion, movement, control, and coordination, and for protection from disease. These systems interact with one another.

BBDCAFE0DFE50131AF3668A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply knowledge of the functions and interconnections of the major human body systems including the breakdown in structure or function that disease causes.

BBDC5E10DFE50131AF3568A86D17958E.description: The number of organisms an ecosystem can support depends on the resources available and abiotic factors, such as quantity of light and water, range of temperatures, and soil composition. Given adequate biotic and abiotic resources and no disease or predators, populations (including humans) increase at rapid rates. Lack of resources and other factors, such as predation and climate, limit the growth of populations in specific niches in the ecosystem.

BBDC1160DFE50131AF3468A86D17958E.description: Chapter 12 of the Iowa Administrative Code states that science instruction shall include conservation of natural resources; and environmental awareness.

BBDBBC70DFE50131AF3368A86D17958E.description: Understand and demonstrate knowledge of the social and personal implications of environmental issues.

BBDB61F0DFE50131AF3268A86D17958E.description: For ecosystems, the major source of energy is sunlight. Energy entering ecosystems as sunlight is transferred by producers into chemical energy through photosynthesis. That energy then passes from organism to organism in food webs.

BBDB1730DFE50131AF3168A86D17958E.description: Biological adaptations include changes in structures, behaviors, or physiology that enhance survival and reproductive success in a particular environment.

BBDACDB0DFE50131AF3068A86D17958E.description: Species acquire many of their unique characteristics through biological adaptation which involves the selection of naturally occurring variations in populations.

BBDA8010DFE50131AF2F68A86D17958E.description: Behavior is one kind of response an organism can make to an internal or environmental stimulus. A behavioral response requires coordination and communication on many levels, including cells, organ systems, and whole organisms. Behavioral response is a set of actions determined in part by heredity and in part from experience.

BBDA3500DFE50131AF2E68A86D17958E.description: Regulation of an organism's internal environment involves sensing the internal environment and changing physiological activities to keep conditions within the range required to survive.

BBD9E820DFE50131AF2D68A86D17958E.description: All organisms must be able to obtain and use resources, grow, reproduce, and maintain stable internal conditions while living in a constantly changing external environment.

BBD99EA0DFE50131AF2C68A86D17958E.description:
Understand and apply knowledge of:
  • interdependency of organisms, changes in environmental conditions, and survival of individuals and species.
  • the cycling of matter and energy in ecosystems.

BBD95730DFE50131AF2B68A86D17958E.description: Living systems at all levels of organization demonstrate the complementary nature of structure and function. Important levels of organization for structure and function include cells, organs, tissues, organ systems, whole organisms, and ecosystems. Organisms are classified according to common characteristics.

BBD90FA0DFE50131AF2A68A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply knowledge of the complementary nature of structure and function and the commonalities among organisms.

BBD8BD20DFE50131AF2968A86D17958E.description: The characteristics of an organism can be described in terms of a combination of traits. Some traits are inherited and others result from interactions with the environment.

BBD87820DFE50131AF2868A86D17958E.description: Hereditary information is contained in genes, located in the chromosomes of each cell. Each gene carries a single unit of information. An inherited trait of an individual can be determined by one or by many genes, and a single gene can influence more than one trait. A human cell contains many thousands of different genes.

BBD833A0DFE50131AF2768A86D17958E.description: Every organism requires a set of instructions for specifying its traits. Heredity is the passage of these instructions from one generation to another.

BBD7EEF0DFE50131AF2668A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply knowledge of how different organisms pass on traits (heredity).

BBD7A800DFE50131AF2568A86D17958E.description: Specialized cells perform specialized functions in multi-cellular organisms. Groups of specialized cells cooperate to form a tissue, such as muscle. Different tissues are, in turn, grouped together to form larger functional units, called organs. Each type of cell, tissue, and organ has a distinct structure and set of functions that serve the organism as a whole.

BBD76030DFE50131AF2468A86D17958E.description: Cells carry on the many functions needed to sustain life. They grow and divide, thereby producing more cells. This requires that they take in nutrients, which they use to provide energy for the work that cells do and to make the materials that a cell or an organism needs.

BBD71190DFE50131AF2368A86D17958E.description: All organisms are composed of cells. Most organisms are single cells; other organisms, including humans are multi-cellular.

BBD6A680DFE50131AF2268A86D17958E.description: Living systems at all levels of organization demonstrate the complementary nature of structure and function. Important levels of organization for structure and function include cells, organs, tissues, organ systems, whole organisms, and ecosystems.

BBD651F0DFE50131AF2168A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply knowledge of the basic components and functions of cells, tissues, organs, and organ systems.

BBD5C140DFE50131AF1F68A86D17958E.description: Most objects in the solar system are in regular and predictable motion. Those motions explain such phenomena as the day, the year, phases of the moon, and eclipses.

BBD57A50DFE50131AF1E68A86D17958E.description: The sun is the major source of energy for phenomena on the earth's surface, such as growth of plants, winds, ocean currents, and the water cycle. Seasons result from variations in the amount of the sun's energy hitting the surface, due to the tilt of the earth's rotation on its axis and the length of the day.

BBD52EE0DFE50131AF1D68A86D17958E.description: Gravity is the force that keeps planets in orbit around the sun and governs the rest of the motion in the solar system. Gravity alone holds us to the earth's surface and explains the phenomena of the tides.

BBD4D640DFE50131AF1C68A86D17958E.description: The earth is the third planet from the sun in a system that includes the moon, the sun, seven other planets and their moons, and smaller objects, such as asteroids and comets. The sun, an average star, is the central and largest body in the solar system.

BBD48D10DFE50131AF1B68A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply knowledge of the components of our solar system.

BBD42950DFE50131AF1A68A86D17958E.description: Clouds, formed by the condensation of water vapor, affect weather and climate.

BBD3C2B0DFE50131AF1968A86D17958E.description: Global patterns of atmospheric movement influence local weather. Oceans have a major effect on climate because water in the oceans holds a large amount of heat.

BBD378F0DFE50131AF1868A86D17958E.description: The atmosphere is a mixture of nitrogen, oxygen, and trace gasses that include water vapor. The atmosphere has different properties at different elevations.

BBD32B40DFE50131AF1768A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply knowledge of the earth's atmospheric properties and how they influence weather and climate.

BBD2E800DFE50131AF1668A86D17958E.description: Fossils provide important evidence of how life and environmental conditions have changed.

BBD2A2D0DFE50131AF1568A86D17958E.description: Earth history is also influenced by occasional catastrophes such as the impact of an asteroid or a comet.

BBD25BA0DFE50131AF1468A86D17958E.description: The earth processes we see today including erosion, movement of tectonic plates, and changes in atmospheric composition are similar to those that occurred in the past.

BBD212B0DFE50131AF1368A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply knowledge of earth history based on physical evidence.

BBD1C290DFE50131AF1268A86D17958E.description: Natural and human forces can contribute to contamination of surface water and groundwater.

BBD16800DFE50131AF1168A86D17958E.description: Water is a solvent. As it passes through the water cycle, especially as it moves on the earth's surface and underground, it dissolves minerals and gases and carries them to the oceans, rivers, and other surface water.

BBD115A0DFE50131AF1068A86D17958E.description: Water, which covers the majority of the earth's surface, circulates through the crust, oceans, and atmosphere in what is known as the "water cycle." Water evaporates from the earth's surface, rises and cools as it rises to higher elevations, condenses as rain or snow, and falls to the surface where it collects in lakes, oceans, soil and in soil and rocks underground.

BBD0CEE0DFE50131AF0F68A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply knowledge of the water cycle, including consideration of events that impact groundwater quality.

BBD08B70DFE50131AF0E68A86D17958E.description: Living organisms have played many roles in the earth system, including affecting the composition of the atmosphere, producing some types of rocks, and contributing to the weathering of rocks.

BBD04520DFE50131AF0D68A86D17958E.description: Soil consists of weathered rocks and decomposed organic matter from dead plants, animals, and bacteria. Soils are often found in layers, with each having a different chemical composition and texture.

BBCFEA10DFE50131AF0C68A86D17958E.description: Some changes in the earth can be described as the "rock cycle." Rocks at the earth's surface weather, forming sediments that are buried, then compacted, heated, and often re-crystallized into new rock. Eventually, those new rocks may be brought to the surface by the forces that drive plate motions, and the rock cycle continues.

BBCF8AE0DFE50131AF0B68A86D17958E.description: Land forms are the result of a combination of constructive and destructive forces. Constructive forces include crustal deformation, volcanic eruption, and deposition of sediment, while destructive forces include weathering and erosion.

BBCF44A0DFE50131AF0A68A86D17958E.description: Tectonic plates constantly move at rates of centimeters per year in response to movements in the mantle. Major geological events, such as earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and mountain building, are results of these plate motions.

BBCEF9F0DFE50131AF0968A86D17958E.description: The solid earth consists of layers including a lithosphere; a hot, convecting mantle and a dense metallic core.

BBCE9B60DFE50131AF0868A86D17958E.description: Understand and apply knowledge of the structure and processes of the earth system and the processes that change the earth and its surface.
